extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in comedy, SNL fans, and pop-culture readers
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing what makes an SNL host 'kill' — qualities of a successful episode and host as described through a report on Betty White's 2010 appearance, focusing on audience reaction, monologue, sketch fit, and viral interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience reaction at dress rehearsal
rubrics_metrics.description: The dress rehearsal response from the studio audience — e.g., 'the dress rehearsal got a huge response from the crowd' and Seth Meyers: 'The hottest dress I was ever at was the Betty White show.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High audience response in dress rehearsal is a key predictor of sketches that will be kept and the overall episode's success; Lorne Michaels uses rehearsal reaction to cut sketches, so a 'killer' dress rehearsal can secure the show regardless of later performance. Example: Michaels went to his office 'because he knew he had the show.' Anti-pattern: weak or tepid rehearsal laughs that lead to cuts or uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monologue effectiveness (self-aware, topical humor)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong monologue that 'dunks on' relevant context — e.g., Betty White's monologue 'found her hilariously dunking on the Facebook fans who wanted her to host the show in the first place.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective monologues play to the host's persona and current cultural context, using self-deprecation or meta-humor to connect with the audience. Example guidance: reference the viral fan campaign in jokes. Anti-pattern: monologues that ignore the host's public image or the episode's promotional narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to fit into and elevate pre-existing sketch molds
rubrics_metrics.description: How well the host integrates into recurring or familiar sketch formats — article: 'she perfectly fit into pre-existing sketch molds, like "The Lawrence Welk Show," "Delicious Dish" and the old census taker bit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hosts who can naturally inhabit established sketch archetypes make sketches land more easily; casting a host who matches sketch tone increases chances of success. Example: playing stock characters convincingly. Anti-pattern: hosts who can't adapt to sketch conventions or who clash with established pacing/voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transforming recurring bits through unexpected casting/interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the host's unique persona to transform a recurring sketch — e.g., Betty White as Kenan Thompson's grandmother 'Loretta' in 'Scared Straight' made the sketch 'destroy at a level I’ve never seen.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casting against type or leveraging a host's unique qualities can revitalize material; extraordinary performances in recurring bits can produce standout moments. Example: a host's personal history or comedic style reframes the sketch's premise. Anti-pattern: treating recurring sketches as rote without tailoring to the host.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leveraging celebrity novelty, nostalgia, and viral interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalizing on public interest and novelty (age, nostalgia, viral campaigns) — e.g., Betty White became 'the oldest person to ever host SNL' after a grassroots Facebook campaign went viral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promoting and incorporating the factors that generated attention (nostalgia, fan campaigns, rarity) can amplify audience engagement; tying jokes to that narrative makes the episode feel timely and relevant. Anti-pattern: ignoring the reasons the audience cares or failing to acknowledge a host's unique backstory.
